The atlasgo.io/features and atlasgo.io/pricing pages give CONFLICTING answers about whether ERD/schema visualization requires a paid plan (see interpretation below) — this conflict is recorded as an open gap, not resolved by picking one page over the other, because both are official Ariga-authored pages of comparable authority and neither is dated. No page was found that explicitly restates, in one place, the exact set of feature rows gated by the 'Atlas MSA'-licensed standard distribution as distinct from the Pro paid-subscription gate — the community-edition page states the Apache-2.0 vs. Atlas-MSA split in general terms (which database engines and 'additional proprietary features') without an exhaustive feature-by-feature table, so the MSA-vs-Pro boundary for individual capabilities is partly inferred by combining two separate pages rather than read off one authoritative table. The Ariga company/funding facts come from secondary press coverage (SiliconANGLE, TechCrunch, Globes, FinSMEs), all evidently derived from the same June 2023 funding-round announcement, so they corroborate rather than independently confirm one another, and are used here only as leads for the governance field's vendor-structure finding, never as sole evidence for a capability claim, per the plan's source_targets constraint.

The standard distribution is built from the same open-source codebase plus some additional proprietary features, and is free to download and use under the terms of the Atlas MSA.

Running `atlas login` unlocks Atlas Pro features such as migration linting, testing, and CI/CD integration. New users get a free 30-day trial, after which a license is required to continue using Atlas Pro.

licence_core_repository.citation: LICENSE file, read directly at raw.githubusercontent.com/ariga/atlas/master/LICENSE, header: 'Apache License Version 2.0'; corroborated by GitHub API license.spdx_id = 'Apache-2.0'
licence_core_repository.rationale: The ariga/atlas GitHub repository's LICENSE file, read directly rather than via GitHub's auto-detected metadata field, is Apache License 2.0 (SPDX identifier Apache-2.0) — an OSI-approved, permissive licence. This answers the source-code-repository licence field precisely and satisfies the plan's requirement to read the LICENSE file directly rather than a third-party summary.

licence_default_distribution_is_not_apac.citation: atlasgo.io/community-edition: 'The standard distribution is built from the same open-source codebase plus some additional proprietary features, and is free to download and use under the terms of the Atlas MSA.'
licence_default_distribution_is_not_apac.rationale: This is the load-bearing finding the task specifically asked for. The Apache-2.0 licence covers only the source repository and a distinct 'Community Edition' build; the binary most users actually install (via the documented default install path, and by extension the unsuffixed/'-extended' Docker Hub tags recorded in the sibling docker-registry facet, as opposed to the '-community' tagged images) is licensed under a separate document Ariga calls the 'Atlas MSA' (Master Subscription/Service Agreement), not Apache-2.0. It is free-to-download and includes 'additional proprietary features' plus a wider set of database drivers (see the Database Support table below), but it is source-available/proprietary-adjacent, not an OSI open-source licence, for anyone running the default distribution rather than deliberately building the Apache-2.0 Community Edition. This directly resolves — as a licensing-level explanation — the open tag-family question the sibling source-atlas-hcl-docker-registry.json record flagged ('the coexistence of unsuffixed, -community, and -extended tag families... was not verified by inspecting image contents'): the '-community' tag family is almost certainly the Apache-2.0 Community Edition build, and the unsuffixed/'-extended' tags are almost certainly the Atlas-MSA-licensed standard distribution, though this record did not independently inspect image manifests/entrypoints to confirm that mapping and states it as a strong inference from the licensing documentation, not a confirmed fact.

licence_pro_paid_tier.citation: atlasgo.io/community-edition ('Running atlas login unlocks Atlas Pro features... a license is required to continue using Atlas Pro'); atlasgo.io/pricing ('Atlas Pro Seats' priced per developer, 30-day free trial then paid); atlasgo.io/features (Pro column)
licence_pro_paid_tier.rationale: On top of the Apache-2.0 core and the free-but-proprietary Atlas-MSA standard distribution, a third, explicitly paid tier ('Atlas Pro', with an 'Enterprise' tier above it) exists, unlocked by logging in and, after a 30-day trial, by a paid subscription (documented elsewhere at $9/seat/month for Pro). This is a three-layer licensing structure, not a simple open-core/paid binary: (1) Apache-2.0 Community Edition, (2) Atlas-MSA standard distribution (free, proprietary, wider driver support), (3) Atlas Pro/Enterprise (paid subscription, additional capabilities).

paid_free_boundary_against_briefs_musts.citation: atlasgo.io/features (CLI Features and Database Support tables) versus atlasgo.io/pricing (Atlas CLI Starter/Pro/Enterprise table) — the two pages disagree on tier gating for at least one of the brief's MUST capabilities
paid_free_boundary_against_briefs_musts.rationale: Schema inspection ('Database Inspection: Open') and the core validator behaviour for the Open-tier database engines are not documented as requiring a paid plan or `atlas login` on either page reviewed; nor is the basic destructive/backward-incompatible/naming-convention lint reported in the sibling source-atlas-hcl-validation-exit.json record as login-gated in its own primary-source excerpt. DDL derivation via `atlas schema apply --dry-run` (sibling record source-atlas-hcl-generation.json, classified expressible) likewise carries no documented login/paid requirement for the Open-tier engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, TiDB, LibSQL); it becomes conditional on a paid plan only if the target database is one of the eleven Pro-only-listed engines (SQL Server, ClickHouse, Redshift, Oracle, Spanner, Snowflake, Databricks, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, Aurora DSQL, Azure Fabric) — which matters here because ADR-0001 leaves the database product unchosen, so this is a conditional, not a settled, answer. Diagram/ERD visualization is the one MUST capability where the two official pages directly conflict: atlasgo.io/features states, verbatim, 'Schema Visualization — Pro Plan Only'; atlasgo.io/pricing's 'Atlas CLI' table lists 'ERD visualization' as included in the Starter (free) column alongside Pro and Enterprise. Neither page is dated, both are equally official (both atlasgo.io, both first-party Ariga documentation), and no third page was found to arbitrate — this is recorded as an unresolved internal inconsistency rather than picked one way. It does not, however, change the sibling source-atlas-hcl-generation.json record's separate, and here uncontested, finding that whichever tier gates it, the visualization mechanism itself routes through Atlas Cloud (the public gh.atlasgo.cloud 'Explore' page or a personal, login-gated workspace) and not a locally-rendered SVG/PNG file — so ERD visualization fails the brief's ephemeral-Docker-container/no-cloud-dependency MUST on that separate, unconflicted ground regardless of which pricing tier answer is correct. The one capability confirmed Pro/Enterprise-only by two independent official pages with no conflict is the custom schema-rule language needed to assert the domain_id cross-cutting convention (already established in source-atlas-hcl-validation-exit.json; corroborated here by atlasgo.io/pricing's and atlasgo.io/features' agreeing 'Custom Schema Rules: Pro' / 'Custom linting rules: Pro' rows).

governance.citation: GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md both confirmed 404 at the repository root of the master branch; GitHub API owner.type = 'Organization' (ariga) with no further documented decision process found; ariga.io's own 'About' page returned no usable governance content when fetched
governance.rationale: No governance charter, steering-council document, BDFL statement, or foundation charter was found for the Atlas project, checked at the two conventional paths and via a general web search. What can be established, from independent funding-news coverage (used here as leads/corroboration only, per the plan's source_targets constraint, never as sole evidence for a capability claim) plus the GitHub organization ownership fact, is vendor structure: Atlas is maintained by a single venture-capital-backed company, Ariga, Inc. (Tel Aviv, Israel; founded 2021 by Ariel Mashraki and Rotem Tamir; approximately $18M raised in an early-stage round led by Tiger Global and TLV Partners, announced June 2023, with total disclosed funding around $30M). This is recorded plainly, per the task's explicit instruction, as single-vendor commercial governance with no foundation or community-consensus structure — the same pattern found for Prisma in the sibling source-prisma-licence-governance.json record, and recorded here as a genuine negative finding for a documented governance process, not inferred as informal community governance from silence.

contrary_evidence_search.result: No GOVERNANCE.md, MAINTAINERS.md, foundation charter, or BDFL statement was found for the Atlas project (confirmed absence via direct 404, not inferred). A genuine, load-bearing complication was found rather than a simple confirmation: the project is not simply 'Apache-2.0, single-vendor' as a first glance at the LICENSE file would suggest — it is a three-tier structure (Apache-2.0 Community Edition / free-but-proprietary Atlas-MSA standard distribution / paid Atlas Pro-Enterprise), and the two official pages documenting which specific capabilities sit in the paid tier (atlasgo.io/features vs atlasgo.io/pricing) directly contradict each other on at least the ERD-visualization row. No evidence of a licence-model change controversy (e.g. a retroactive move to a more restrictive licence for the core Apache-2.0 repository itself) was found; the LICENSE file at the current retrieval date is unambiguously Apache-2.0 for the core repository.
